passage:
"Thomas, why are you glaring at Ruchika?"
"Santosh, you haven't heard? Voice note in the class group. Her voice, calling the new girl names. Horrible stuff."
"Play it."
"...See? That's literally her voice. The way she says 'yaar' and everything."
"Hmm. It says Friday evening. Ruchika was at the district match all Friday, till nine."
"So she recorded it on the bus."
"No crowd, no bus noise. And listen, she never pauses to breathe. Voices can be made now, Thomas. You just need clips of someone talking."
"But it sounds exactly like her."
"That's the point. Sounding like her isn't proof it's her."
Thomas stared at his phone for a long moment. "I already replied 'disgusting' to it."
"Delete that. Then let's show Kurian ma'am."
Mrs Kurian listened twice, took screenshots and said, "Thank you both. Nobody forwards this. I'm speaking to the counsellor and Ruchika's parents today."

qa.q: Where was Ruchika all Friday, according to Santosh?
qa.a: Santosh says Ruchika was at the district match all Friday, till nine.

qa.q: Why was Thomas so sure the voice note was real?
qa.a: Thomas trusted his ears; the voice, and even the way it said "yaar", sounded exactly like Ruchika, so he felt it had to be her.

qa.q: Which steps did Thomas and Santosh take once they doubted the note?
qa.a: Thomas deleted the angry reply, and they took the voice note to Mrs Kurian instead of forwarding it.

qa.q: What is it like for Ruchika while the voice note spreads?
qa.a: Ruchika is glared at and judged for words she may never have said, before anyone checks where she was that evening.

grounding: A teenager believes a voice note of Ruchika because it sounds exactly like her, until the timing and oddities show the recording itself is not proof.

passage:
I was fifteen when I saw the video of the famous singer laughing at our town after the floods. It was everywhere. His face, his voice, his usual black kurta. "Those people deserve it," he said, and smirked.
I was furious. Our school had been a shelter for two weeks. I posted a long angry comment and made Samir watch it at recess. "He actually said it, look at his mouth."
Three days later a news channel showed the real clip. He had been talking about a cricket match. Someone had taken his face and voice and made new words come out.
I watched the fake again and saw things I had missed: the lips a little late, the blink that never came. The first time, nobody noticed.
I deleted my comment. Samir said, "It looked real to me too."
What stuck with me was that seeing it had once been enough.
Manoj

qa.q: How long had Manoj's school been a shelter?
qa.a: The school had been a shelter for two weeks.

qa.q: Why was Manoj so ready to believe the video?
qa.a: Manoj was already hurt and angry about the floods, and the video showed the singer's own face and voice, so it felt like proof.

qa.q: What turning point changed Manoj's view of the video?
qa.a: The news channel showing the real clip, about a cricket match, revealed that the face and voice had been used to make new words.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt when Manoj showed the video at recess?
qa.a: Samir was probably pulled into the anger too, and the line "It looked real to me too" shows Samir was just as fooled.

grounding: A teenager believes a fake video of a famous singer because it looks and sounds real, and later learns the medium itself is no longer proof.

passage:
"You said I'm fake and everyone only tolerates me." Dolma held out her phone. "It's your voice, Devika. Forty people have heard it."
"I never said that!"
"It's your voice. Your laugh at the end."
"Play it again." Devika listened, going pale. "That's how I sound... but I didn't. I swear. Where did it come from?"
"Someone sent it in the class group at midnight. No name."
"Dolma, last week someone sent me a link for a 'funny voice test'. I recorded a few lines. I thought it was a game."
They stood there, both shaking.
"Let's go to Ms Rao. Now."
In the staffroom, Ms Rao listened to the clip twice. "Voices can be copied now, girls. I believe you both. I'm taking this to the counsellor and the principal this afternoon, and I'll ask the group admin to take it down right away. Dolma, this is not your fault. And Devika, it isn't yours either."

qa.q: When was the voice note sent in the class group?
qa.a: Someone sent it in the class group at midnight, with no name.

qa.q: Why did Dolma believe the voice note at first, and how did it make her feel?
qa.a: Dolma felt hurt and betrayed; it was Devika's voice and laugh, so it seemed like proof.

qa.q: What did Ms Rao do that helped Dolma and Devika?
qa.a: Ms Rao listened twice, explained that voices can be copied, believed them both, and took it to the counsellor and principal that afternoon while asking for the clip to be taken down.

qa.q: What is it like for Devika to hear her own voice saying things she never said?
qa.a: Devika went pale and shaky; being blamed by a clip that sounds exactly like her is frightening and hard to disprove alone.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing a fake voice note of a classmate because it sounds real, and learning that a recording is no longer proof.

passage:
I'm Kunal, and I used to say, "I'll believe it when I see it." Not anymore.
Last month a video went round our tuition group: a famous film actor, the one in every biscuit ad, saying our state's board exams would be cancelled and everyone would simply pass. His face, his voice, his usual hand wave. I believed it completely. I even stopped revising for two days.
Anirban was the one who said, "Watch his mouth." When the actor said "cancelled", his lips moved a tiny bit late. His earring blinked in and out. Anirban checked the actor's own page and the board's website. Nothing. The board had a notice up: "Fake video circulating."
I felt stupid, and a bit scared. If a face and a voice can be made up that well, what else have I believed?
Now when something looks shocking, I check where it first came from before I trust my own eyes.

qa.q: What did the video claim about the board exams?
qa.a: That the board exams would be cancelled and everyone would simply pass.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel after learning the video was fake?
qa.a: Kunal felt stupid and a bit scared, wondering what else had been believed just because a face and voice looked real.

qa.q: Which checks did Anirban use, and what can Kunal do next time?
qa.a: Watching the lip timing and the blinking earring, then checking the actor's own page and the board's website; Kunal can now check where something first came from.

qa.q: What would change if Anirban had not been in the group?
qa.a: Kunal might have kept skipping revision, trusting the video, until the real exams arrived.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing a fake video of a famous actor because it looked and sounded real, and learning the medium is no longer proof.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Monday
Imran (Class 11) came in at lunch, angry and close to tears. He showed me a short video in which Shankar, his closest friend, seemed to say, "Imran only got into the team because his dad knows the coach." Imran had watched it maybe twenty times. "It's his face, ma'am. It's him."
I asked Imran to watch it with the sound off. The background was our basketball court, but the shadows fell the wrong way for that time of day, and Shankar's collar changed shape between two frames. Imran went quiet.
What I did next: I called Shankar in separately. He was shocked and said he had never said it. With both boys' agreement I informed the principal and our safeguarding lead the same afternoon, reported the account that posted it, and called both families. I will meet the boys together tomorrow.

qa.q: How many times had Imran watched the video?
qa.a: Imran had watched it maybe twenty times.

qa.q: How was Imran feeling when he came in at lunch?
qa.a: Imran was angry and close to tears, hurt that his closest friend seemed to mock him on video.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take the same day?
qa.a: Checked the video with Imran, spoke to Shankar separately, informed the principal and safeguarding lead, reported the account and called both families.

qa.q: What would it be like for Shankar to learn about the video?
qa.a: Shankar was shocked to see his own face saying words he never said, and could have lost his closest friend over it.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing a fake video of his friend because it looked real, and a counsellor showing why video is no longer proof.

passage:
Tuesday
This morning a voice note went round the class group: Sumit's voice, calling Mrs D'Souza names I won't write here. It was so clearly him, the way he says "basically", the little laugh. I believed it straight away. I even sent an angry reply.
At break Sumit was white as chalk. He said he never said it, and he was shaking. I didn't believe him at first. Then he showed our class teacher, and Mr Ansari played it on the laptop, slowed down. There were odd gaps, and one word sounded pasted in. He said voices can be copied now from old clips, and videos too. By lunch he had taken it to the principal, asked the group admin to delete it, and told us all to stop sharing.
I feel awful. I heard it with my own ears, and my ears were wrong. From now on, hearing isn't proof. I owe Sumit an apology. Not tomorrow. I'm messaging him now.
Rajni

qa.q: What did Mr Ansari do with the voice note?
qa.a: He played it on the laptop, slowed down.

qa.q: How does Rajni feel after learning the note was fake?
qa.a: Rajni feels awful and guilty for believing it and sending an angry reply, shaken that even one's own ears can be wrong.

qa.q: What will Rajni do now, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Rajni is apologising to Sumit right away and will no longer treat audio or video as proof by itself, which stops adding to the harm.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit was white and shaking, accused of words he never said and not believed at first by classmates.

grounding: Shows a teenager who believed a faked voice note of a classmate because it sounded real, learning that the medium itself is no longer proof.
